title: Customise the harness only where the contract demands it · Workflow patterns
description: Choose customisation by a clear contract, measurable benefit and manageable maintenance burden. Select and combine workflow patterns for proposals, reviews, scheduled maintenance and gated release.

sections.title: Customise the harness only where the contract demands it
sections.navLabel: Customise the harness only where the contract demands it

blocks.body:
Your team requires every write to go through an audited transaction service. The current agent can edit files directly, but its supported configuration cannot route writes through that service. There is a specific gap worth addressing.

Compare that with replacing a harness because its internal API is not how you would have designed it. Both projects can produce satisfying code. Only the first starts with a requirement the current system cannot meet. Customisation is easiest to justify when you can name that requirement and test it.

blocks.title: The default runner cannot expose a stable diff after a long task.
blocks.problem: The default runner cannot expose a stable diff after a long task.

steps.title: Name the gap
steps.body: The team needs resumable state and a reviewable patch, but the default runner returns only a final message.
steps.reason: The custom requirement is about evidence and recovery.
steps.trap: Building a new orchestration framework before proving the gap.

steps.title: Add the smallest adapter
steps.body: Persist the revision, checkpoint and diff artifact, then test timeout and resume behaviour.
steps.reason: The change improves the contract without replacing the whole harness.
steps.trap: Hiding the adapter's configuration in an opaque service.

blocks.title: Start with the unmet contract
blocks.body: Name the failure of the current harness: missing repository state, unsafe permissions, poor output, no resume path or an untestable side effect. Then define the smallest addition that fixes it. Preserve familiar interfaces where possible so the custom piece reduces cognitive load instead of adding a private dialect.

blocks.bridge: Customisation should answer a real contract gap.
blocks.meaning: A new abstraction earns its place when it improves safety, evidence or repeatability in a measurable way.
blocks.question: A team wants a custom agent wrapper because its name sounds nicer. Is that enough?
blocks.answer: No. It needs a concrete problem and a benefit worth the implementation and maintenance cost.

further.question: What is a good reason to customise?
further.answer: The default cannot expose a required invariant, enforce a permission boundary or support a repeatable verification path.

further.question: Why keep interfaces familiar?
further.answer: Familiar shapes reduce training, integration and migration cost.

blocks.title: Measure the trade
blocks.body: A custom harness has acquisition cost, maintenance cost and migration risk. Compare those with the recurring cost of the problem it solves. Keep configuration explicit, test failure paths and provide a fallback or removal plan if the underlying platform changes.

blocks.bridge: Every custom layer becomes part of the system you must understand.
blocks.meaning: Maintenance and failure behaviour are part of the design, not an afterthought.
blocks.question: What should accompany a custom harness component?
blocks.answer: A focused contract, tests for denial and failure, explicit configuration and a plan for updating or removing it.

further.question: What is migration risk?
further.answer: The chance that the custom layer becomes a dependency that blocks a platform or model change.

further.question: When should a customisation be removed?
further.answer: When the underlying platform now supplies the contract reliably or the maintenance cost exceeds the recurring benefit.

blocks.body: Customise for a measurable contract gap, and keep the new layer small, explicit and removable.
blocks.nextConnection: The final lesson turns these principles into recurring workflow shapes that teams can operate without improvising every run.

sections.title: Workflow patterns: make the boring path reliable

blocks.body: Most useful automation is deliberately boring. It notices a known event, gathers bounded evidence, produces a familiar artefact and asks for the next decision in a predictable place. Patterns help teams recognise that shape instead of inventing a new control model for every job.

blocks.title: Choose the shape before the implementation
blocks.body: A proposal workflow reads inputs and creates a draft. A review workflow gathers evidence around a change. A scheduled maintenance workflow checks for drift and opens a bounded issue or patch. A gated release workflow carries a reviewed result across an approval boundary. The pattern determines where state, evidence and authority should live.

blocks.bridge: A workflow pattern is a control shape, not a branded recipe.
blocks.meaning: Choose it by the kind of effect and decision the workflow needs to support.
blocks.question: Which pattern fits a nightly scan that should propose dependency updates for review?
blocks.answer: Scheduled maintenance producing a bounded proposal or issue, with merge and release kept behind review.

further.question: What is a proposal workflow for?
further.answer: Turning an investigation into a reviewable artifact without applying the consequential change automatically.

further.question: What makes a release workflow gated?
further.answer: The reviewed result crosses an explicit approval boundary before external or production effect.

blocks.title: A team wants automated stale-issue triage.
blocks.problem: A team wants automated stale-issue triage.

steps.title: Pick the pattern
steps.body: Use an event-triggered proposal workflow: classify the issue, attach evidence and draft a label or comment for review.
steps.reason: The effect is bounded and familiar.
steps.trap: Letting the agent close issues directly on its first run.

steps.title: Make reruns safe
steps.body: Use the issue ID and a comment marker to update the existing proposal instead of creating duplicates.
steps.reason: The workflow can recover from delivery retries.
steps.trap: Treating every trigger as a brand-new task.

blocks.title: Compose with explicit handoffs
blocks.body:
Imagine a scheduled investigator opens an issue, then loses its connection before recording success. The scheduler retries. If the second run simply opens another issue, a successful action has become a duplicate.

Give the logical operation a stable identity, such as the repository, failing check and revision. Before publishing again, use that identity to reconcile the existing output. If the destination supports an idempotency key, repeated requests can refer to the same operation. Otherwise the workflow needs its own durable record and a way to check an uncertain result.

A lookup followed by a write can still race when two runs overlap. Use a suitable lock, uniqueness constraint or destination guarantee where needed. The important handoff includes not just the report, but enough identity and status to distinguish 'not attempted' from 'may already have happened'.

blocks.bridge: Reliable patterns make retries and handoffs ordinary.
blocks.meaning: Stable identifiers and explicit status stop a partially completed run from becoming duplicate or invisible work.
blocks.question: A network retry repeats a workflow after the draft already exists. What should the design use?
blocks.answer: An idempotency key or stable task identifier that lets the workflow find and update the existing artifact.

further.question: Why make handoffs explicit?
further.answer: Each stage can show what evidence and authority it received instead of inheriting hidden assumptions.

further.question: What should status distinguish?
further.answer: Operational state, such as timed out, from task state, such as proposal ready or verification failed.

data.title: Lab 6 · Design an unattended workflow
data.brief: Choose a recurring repository event and design the smallest workflow that can investigate, produce evidence and stop safely.
steps: Draw the trigger, checkout, instructions, tools, identity, output and approval boundary.
Set duration, retry, spend and concurrency controls with a response for each limit.
Choose a workflow pattern and add an idempotency key or stable task identifier.
Run a happy path and one timeout or duplicate-delivery simulation.
data.review: The design should make it clear what can happen without approval, what evidence is produced and how a retry avoids duplicate effects. A schedule plus a prompt is not yet an operating workflow.

blocks.body: Choose a workflow shape that makes evidence, handoffs, retries and approval boundaries predictable.

data.governingLaw: A custom workflow is a new system with its own contract, state transitions, tool policy, and evaluation burden. A workflow pattern is a reusable arrangement of trigger, state, action, evidence, and human intervention.
data.invariant: Custom behaviour must preserve the platform's event identity, permission, and completion semantics or document the change. The pattern's acceptance condition must remain independent of the agent's own completion claim.
data.limitingCase: If the platform already expresses the required contract, custom code adds maintenance without capability gain. A manual step is preferable when the automated path costs more to operate than the work it replaces.
data.counterexample: A shorter custom path can be less reliable when it removes the platform's verification or retry semantics. Adding parallel branches can increase coordination and merge failure enough to reduce total throughput.
data.validity: Customisation is justified only by a measured requirement the existing path cannot satisfy. Patterns transfer only when their event, authority, evidence, and failure assumptions transfer too.
